title: OEE Calculator in Excel with Weighted Line Roll-up (Availability, Performance, Quality)
summary: Excel log sheet and summary that calculate availability, performance, quality and OEE per shift, check for impossible values, and roll up per line with sums instead of averaging percentages.
body:
## What it does
Calculates OEE per shift from five inputs (planned minutes, downtime minutes, ideal cycle time, total parts, good parts), flags impossible data, and rolls up per line correctly. The roll-up uses sums, because averaging the OEE percentages of shifts with different planned times gives a wrong number. It works in every Excel version with SUMIFS (Excel 2007 and later). No dynamic arrays needed.

## Definitions used
- Run time = planned time minus downtime.
- Availability = run time / planned time.
- Ideal minutes = total parts x ideal cycle time (s) / 60.
- Performance = ideal minutes / run time.
- Quality = good parts / total parts.
- OEE = availability x performance x quality = (good parts x ideal cycle time / 60) / planned time.
Agree the definition of planned time and of the ideal cycle time in your plant before comparing lines. Document it on the sheet.

## Sheet OEE_Log (row 1 headers, data from row 2)
A Date, B Line, C Shift, D Planned min, E Downtime min, F Ideal cycle s, G Total parts, H Good parts. Calculated columns, entered in row 2 and filled down:

```
I2: =D2-E2
J2: =F2*G2/60
K2: =IF(D2>0,I2/D2,"")
L2: =IF(I2>0,J2/I2,"")
M2: =IF(G2>0,H2/G2,"")
N2: =IF(COUNT(K2:M2)=3,K2*L2*M2,"")
O2: =IF(H2>G2,"Good > total",IF(E2>D2,"Downtime > planned",IF(L2>1,"Performance > 100%: check ideal cycle","OK")))
```
Format K to N as percent. Column O is the data quality check. Performance above 100 percent almost always means the ideal cycle time is too slow or the part count includes something it should not.

## Sheet Summary (one row per line, lines typed in column A from row 2)
```
B2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$D$2:$D$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
C2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$I$2:$I$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
D2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$J$2:$J$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
E2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$G$2:$G$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
F2: =SUMIFS(OEE_Log!$H$2:$H$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
G2: =C2/B2
H2: =D2/C2
I2: =F2/E2
J2: =G2*H2*I2
K2: =AVERAGEIFS(OEE_Log!$N$2:$N$500,OEE_Log!$B$2:$B$500,$A2)
```
Headers for B to K: Planned min, Run min, Ideal min, Total, Good, Availability, Performance, Quality, OEE, Simple average (for comparison only). If your data will grow beyond row 500, convert the log to a Table (Ctrl+T) and use structured references or extend the ranges.

## Worked example (invented data, 2 March)
| Line | Shift | Planned | Down | Ideal s | Total | Good | Run | Ideal min | A | P | Q | OEE |
| L1 | Early | 450 | 54 | 40 | 480 | 456 | 396 | 320.0 | 88.0% | 80.8% | 95.0% | 67.6% |
| L1 | Late | 450 | 90 | 40 | 380 | 349 | 360 | 253.3 | 80.0% | 70.4% | 91.8% | 51.7% |
| L1 | Night | 240 | 20 | 40 | 320 | 312 | 220 | 213.3 | 91.7% | 97.0% | 97.5% | 86.7% |
| L2 | Early | 450 | 45 | 60 | 300 | 291 | 405 | 300.0 | 90.0% | 74.1% | 97.0% | 64.7% |
| L2 | Late | 450 | 120 | 60 | 210 | 195 | 330 | 210.0 | 73.3% | 63.6% | 92.9% | 43.3% |

Roll-up L1: planned 1,140, run 976, ideal 786.7, total 1,180, good 1,117. Availability 976 / 1,140 = 85.6 percent, performance 786.7 / 976 = 80.6 percent, quality 1,117 / 1,180 = 94.7 percent, OEE = 65.3 percent. Cross-check: 1,117 x 40 / 60 / 1,140 = 65.3 percent. The simple average of the three shift OEE values is 68.6 percent, 3.3 points too high, because the short night shift with its good result has the same weight as a full shift. L2 roll-up: 900 planned, 735 run, 510 ideal, 510 total, 486 good, A 81.7 percent, P 69.4 percent, Q 95.3 percent, OEE 54.0 percent.

## How to adapt
- Add a column for planned stops if you want to separate them from downtime.
- Add reason columns (breakdown, changeover, minor stops) and use the minutes-based loss view: every loss in minutes, as a share of planned time.
- Use conditional formatting on column N with thresholds that your plant sets. Do not copy a world-class value from the internet without agreeing it locally.
- For several machines per line, add a Machine column and a second SUMIFS criterion.

## Common mistakes
- Averaging percentages of unequal shifts (see example).
- Changing the ideal cycle time to improve the score. Keep one documented reference, for example the best demonstrated rate, and change it only with a note.
- Entering downtime in hours in one row and minutes in another.
- Counting parts that are reworked later as good parts, in some shifts and not in others.
- Text numbers: if a value is left-aligned and SUMIFS ignores it, convert it with Data > Text to Columns.

## Data protection and safety
The sheet contains machine and shift data. If shift names or operator names are added, remember that OEE by person is performance data of employees and needs the works council and data protection involved. Store the file in a SharePoint library with the right permissions, not on a USB stick. The numbers support improvement work; they are not a quality record for released parts.

title: Value Stream Table in Excel: Lead Time, Queue Days, Value-Added Ratio and Bottleneck
summary: Excel sheet for a current-state value stream: takt, queue days from WIP, lead time, value-added ratio and the bottleneck step by effective cycle time, using only classic functions.
body:
## What it does
Holds the numbers behind a current-state value stream map and calculates takt time, effective cycle time per step, queue time in days, total lead time, value-added ratio and the bottleneck. It makes the typical finding visible: lead time is mostly waiting, not working. It uses only SUM, MAX, INDEX and MATCH, so it works in any Excel version.

## Layout (sheet VSM)
Inputs at the top:
```
A1: Demand per day (pcs)           B1: 200
A2: Available time per day (s)     B2: 27000
A3: Takt time (s)                  B3: =B2/B1
```
Step table, headers in row 5, steps in rows 6 to 10 (add rows and extend the ranges for more steps). Columns A to E are typed: Step, Cycle time s, Value-adding (Y or N), Uptime (fraction), WIP before step (pieces). Columns F to H are formulas:
```
F6: =B6/D6            effective cycle time
G6: =E6/$B$1          queue days (WIP divided by daily demand)
H6: =IF(C6="Y",B6,0)  value-adding seconds
```
Fill F6:H6 down. Results below the table:
```
B12: =SUM(B6:B10)                       total processing time (s)
B13: =SUM(G6:G10)                       total queue (days)
B14: =B13+B12/B2                        lead time (working days)
B15: =SUM(H6:H10)                       value-adding time (s)
B16: =B15/(B14*B2)                      value-added ratio
B17: =INDEX(A6:A10,MATCH(MAX(F6:F10),F6:F10,0))   bottleneck step
B18: =MAX(F6:F10)                       bottleneck effective CT (s)
B19: =B18/B3                            bottleneck load vs takt
```
Format B16 and B19 as percent with two decimals (B16 is tiny).

## Worked example (invented data)
Demand 200 pieces per day, 27,000 s available, takt = 135 s.
| Step | CT s | VA | Uptime | WIP | Effective CT | Queue days |
| Cut | 38 | Y | 90% | 800 | 42.2 | 4.0 |
| Drill | 52 | Y | 95% | 600 | 54.7 | 3.0 |
| Deburr | 45 | N | 92% | 400 | 48.9 | 2.0 |
| Inspect | 30 | N | 100% | 200 | 30.0 | 1.0 |
| Pack | 20 | N | 100% | 100 | 20.0 | 0.5 |

Processing time 185 s. Queue 10.5 days. Lead time = 10.5 + 185 / 27,000 = 10.507 days. Value-adding time 90 s (Cut and Drill), so value-added ratio = 90 / (10.507 x 27,000) = 0.032 percent. Bottleneck: Drill at 54.7 s, which is 40.6 percent of takt. Reading: capacity is no problem, the process waits. Reducing WIP before each step to 100 pieces (half a day of demand, an assumption) would cut queue to 2.5 days.

## How to adapt
- Batch processes: add a batch size column and use cycle time per piece = batch time / batch size.
- Changeover: add a changeover column and divide it by the lot size to get the contribution per piece.
- Steps in parallel: enter the combined cycle time (cycle time divided by the number of identical machines) if they share one queue.
- Future state: copy the sheet, change WIP and uptime, and compare lead time in a small table.

## Common mistakes
- Queue days from WIP divided by daily output instead of daily demand. If the line is behind, output differs from demand; choose one and say which.
- Uptime entered as 90 instead of 0.9 (cycle time is then divided by 90).
- Marking inspection or documentation as value-adding. Required, but not value-adding.
- Reading the value-added ratio as precise. It is an order of magnitude; the point is the difference between waiting and working.
- Mixing working days and calendar days in the lead time. Use working days and state it.

## Data protection and safety
The data are process data. Do not publish customer-confidential part numbers in a shared workbook outside the people who need them. A value stream table supports a workshop; any change to a regulated process (for example in aircraft production or maintenance) still goes through the normal change control and quality approval.

title: SMED Changeover Sheet in Excel: Internal vs External Time, Savings and Freed Capacity
summary: Excel sheet for a SMED study: classify each changeover element as internal or external before and after, and calculate machine downtime saved, percent reduction and freed capacity per week.
body:
## What it does
SMED means reducing changeover time by separating internal elements (done while the machine is stopped) from external ones (done while it runs) and then shortening both. This sheet lists each element of a changeover, records its type and duration now and in the proposed state, and calculates how much stopped time is saved. It uses SUMIFS and COUNTIFS (Excel 2007 and later). One optional formula needs Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365.

## Layout (sheet SMED)
Row 1 headers: A #, B Element, C Current type, D Current s, E Proposed type, F Proposed s. Elements from row 2 to row 11 (extend as needed). Types are typed as Internal or External. Add a drop-down: select C2:C11 and E2:E11, Data > Data Validation > List, source: Internal,External. This avoids typos that SUMIFS would silently ignore.

Parameters and results in columns H and I:
```
I1: 6                                           changeovers per week
I2: 40                                          cycle time (s per part)
I4: =SUMIFS(D2:D11,C2:C11,"Internal")           internal time now (s)
I5: =SUMIFS(F2:F11,E2:E11,"Internal")           internal time proposed (s)
I6: =I4-I5                                      reduction (s)
I7: =IF(I4>0,I6/I4,0)                           reduction (%)
I8: =COUNTIFS(C2:C11,"Internal",E2:E11,"External")   elements moved to external
I9: =SUMIFS(D2:D11,C2:C11,"Internal",E2:E11,"External")   seconds moved to external
I10: =I6*I1/60                                  machine minutes freed per week
I11: =I6*I1/I2                                  extra parts per week (upper bound)
```
Optional list of moved elements (Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365, spills): `=FILTER(B2:B11,(C2:C11="Internal")*(E2:E11="External"),"none")`. In older versions use a filter on the table instead.

## Worked example (invented data, CNC changeover)
| # | Element | Now | s | Proposed | s |
| 1 | Fetch fixture from tool crib | Internal | 300 | External | 300 |
| 2 | Stop machine, clear chips | Internal | 120 | Internal | 90 |
| 3 | Remove old fixture | Internal | 240 | Internal | 150 |
| 4 | Clean machine table | Internal | 180 | Internal | 120 |
| 5 | Stage new program and NC data | Internal | 150 | External | 150 |
| 6 | Mount new fixture | Internal | 420 | Internal | 240 |
| 7 | Set work offsets (touch-off) | Internal | 360 | Internal | 180 |
| 8 | Load program, dry run | Internal | 300 | Internal | 180 |
| 9 | First-off inspection | Internal | 600 | Internal | 540 |
| 10 | Prepare job documents | Internal | 180 | External | 180 |

Results: internal time now = 2,850 s (47.5 min). Proposed internal time = 90 + 150 + 120 + 240 + 180 + 180 + 540 = 1,500 s (25 min). Reduction 1,350 s = 47.4 percent. Three elements move to external, 630 s (300 + 150 + 180). With 6 changeovers per week: 1,350 x 6 / 60 = 135 machine minutes freed. At 40 s per part this is at most 1,350 x 6 / 40 = 202.5 additional parts per week, an upper bound that assumes the machine has demand and material for them.

## How to adapt
- Record the real durations from a video of one changeover, not from memory. Time each element once, then average several changeovers.
- Add a column Owner (role) and one for the improvement idea per element.
- Add a changeover cost: freed minutes times your machine hour rate, if finance agrees on the rate.
- Keep the same sheet per machine family; do not mix different changeover types in one list.

## Common mistakes
- Moving an element to External without anyone available to do it while the machine runs. The time does not disappear, the operator just does it later.
- Typing "internal" in one cell and "Internal " (trailing space) in another. Use the drop-down.
- Cutting inspection or release steps to reach a number. In regulated production, first-off or first-article checks stay; the quality function decides what can be prepared in advance. In aircraft maintenance, tool and torque checks follow approved procedures and are not SMED candidates.
- Reading the extra-parts figure as a promise.
- Adding the durations of external elements to the downtime. Only internal ones stop the machine.

## Data protection and safety
The sheet holds process data. If the changeover video shows people, check consent and works council agreements before storing or sharing it. Safety steps (lock-out, guards) are never shortened or reordered by a spreadsheet; the safety officer reviews any change to the changeover sequence.

title: Takt Time and Line Balancing Sheet in Excel with Station Load and Balance Efficiency
summary: Excel sheet that calculates takt time from shift data and yield, sums task times per station, flags stations over takt, and shows minimum stations and balance efficiency before and after a rebalance.
body:
## What it does
Calculates takt time from your shift pattern and demand, adds up task times per station, shows each station's utilisation of takt, flags stations that cannot keep up, and gives the minimum number of stations and the balance efficiency. It uses SUMIFS, ROUNDUP, MAX and COUNTIF, so it works in every Excel version since 2007.

## Layout (sheet Takt)
Inputs in A1:B6:
```
B1: 480     shift length (min)
B2: 45      breaks per shift (min)
B3: 15      huddle and cleaning per shift (min)
B4: 2       shifts per day
B5: 360     good units required per day
B6: 0.975   expected yield (fraction)
B8:  =(B1-B2-B3)*B4*60     net available time per day (s)
B9:  =B5/B6                units to start per day
B10: =B8/B9                takt time (s)
```
Task list in D1:F11 (headers Task, Time s, Station), one row per task with the station it is assigned to. Station table in H1:K5 for stations 1 to 4 (extend for more):
```
I2: =SUMIFS($E$2:$E$11,$F$2:$F$11,H2)      station load (s)
J2: =I2/$B$10                               utilisation of takt
K2: =IF(I2>$B$10,"Over takt","OK")
```
Fill down to row 5. Summary:
```
B12: =SUM(E2:E11)                total task time (s)
B13: =ROUNDUP(B12/B10,0)         minimum number of stations
B14: =COUNT(H2:H5)               stations used
B15: =MAX(I2:I5)                 slowest station load (s)
B16: =B12/(B14*B15)              balance efficiency
B17: =1-B16                      balance loss
B18: =COUNTIF(K2:K5,"Over takt") stations over takt
```

## Worked example (invented data)
Net available time = (480 - 45 - 15) x 2 x 60 = 50,400 s. Good units 360 at yield 97.5 percent means 360 / 0.975 = 369.2 units to start. Takt = 50,400 / 369.23 = 136.5 s.

Tasks (s): T1 22, T2 36, T3 30, T4 30, T5 44, T6 52, T7 44, T8 40, T9 62, T10 70. Assignment A: station 1 gets T1 to T4, station 2 gets T5 to T7, station 3 gets T8 and T9, station 4 gets T10.
| Station | Load s | Utilisation of takt | Flag |
| 1 | 118 | 86.4% | OK |
| 2 | 140 | 102.6% | Over takt |
| 3 | 102 | 74.7% | OK |
| 4 | 70 | 51.3% | OK |

Total task time 430 s, 430 / 136.5 = 3.15, so the minimum is 4 stations. Balance efficiency = 430 / (4 x 140) = 76.8 percent, balance loss 23.2 percent, one station over takt.

Rebalance: move T7 (44 s) from station 2 to station 4, assuming the task sequence allows it. Loads become 118, 96, 102 and 114 s. Slowest 118 s, efficiency = 430 / (4 x 118) = 91.1 percent, no station over takt. Change cell F8 from 2 to 4 and the sheet shows it at once.

## How to adapt
- Different shift patterns: put each pattern in its own column and calculate takt per pattern.
- Add a column for the predecessor of each task and check by eye or with a second column that no task sits at an earlier station than its predecessor.
- Add a buffer target, for example plan stations at 90 percent of takt, as an input cell that replaces $B$10 in the flag formula, if your plant uses such a rule.
- For mixed models, use a weighted average task time per station from the product mix.

## Common mistakes
- Using gross shift time instead of net available time. Breaks and planned stops belong out of the denominator.
- Taking takt equal to cycle time. Takt is demand-driven; cycle time is what the process delivers.
- Forgetting yield, so the line is planned for good units but has to start more.
- Balancing to 100 percent of takt without any allowance for disturbance.
- Moving tasks without checking sequence, tools, ergonomics and qualifications. In aircraft assembly and maintenance, task order is often fixed by approved documents, and who may do a task is fixed by authorisation; the sheet cannot decide that.

## Data protection and safety
The sheet contains time data per task, not per person. Do not add operator names to station loads: station times used for individual assessment are performance data and need works council involvement. Ergonomic and safety limits stay with the responsible specialists.

title: 5S Scorecard in Excel with Area Matrix, Weights and Latest Audit per Area
summary: Excel workbook that stores 5S audit answers as rows, calculates percent per S and per area for a chosen audit date with optional weights, and finds the latest audit date per area.
body:
## What it does
Stores each audit answer as one row (date, area, S, question, score 0 to 4) and builds a matrix of areas by S for a chosen audit date. Because the scores are rows, you can add or remove questions without breaking formulas, and each S is divided by its own number of questions. It uses SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and SUMPRODUCT (Excel 2007 and later). The latest-audit column uses MAXIFS, which needs Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365.

## Sheet Answers (row 1 headers)
A Date, B Area, C S, D Question, E Score. The S column must contain exactly the names used in the matrix headers: Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain. Add data validation for E (Data > Data Validation > Whole number between 0 and 4) and a list for C. Scale used here: 0 = not in place, 2 = partly, 4 = in place and held; define your own wording in the audit instructions.

## Sheet Matrix
```
A1: Audit date    B1: 2026-03-09   (a real date)
Row 3 headers: A3 Area, B3 Sort, C3 Set in order, D3 Shine, E3 Standardise, F3 Sustain, G3 Weighted total, H3 Latest audit
Row 4: A4 Weight, B4 1, C4 1, D4 1, E4 2, F4 2          (weights are an example, set your own)
A5: Machining cell 1     A6: Assembly bay 2

B5: =IFERROR(SUMIFS(Answers!$E$2:$E$1000,Answers!$B$2:$B$1000,$A5,Answers!$C$2:$C$1000,B$3,Answers!$A$2:$A$1000,$B$1)/(4*COUNTIFS(Answers!$B$2:$B$1000,$A5,Answers!$C$2:$C$1000,B$3,Answers!$A$2:$A$1000,$B$1)),"")
G5: =IFERROR(SUMPRODUCT(B5:F5,$B$4:$F$4)/SUM($B$4:$F$4),"")
H5: =MAXIFS(Answers!$A$2:$A$1000,Answers!$B$2:$B$1000,$A5)
```
Fill B5 across to F5, then rows 5 to 6 down (and further for more areas). Format B to G as percent and H as date. If an S was not scored the cell shows empty, and SUMPRODUCT then treats it as zero, so for partial audits compare only complete audits. For equal weights set B4:F4 to 1.

## Worked example (invented data, audit of 9 March 2026)
Three questions per S. Machining cell 1: Sort 3, 4, 3; Set in order 2, 3, 3; Shine 4, 3, 3; Standardise 2, 2, 1; Sustain 1, 2, 2. Assembly bay 2: Sort 4, 4, 3; Set in order 3, 4, 4; Shine 3, 3, 4; Standardise 3, 3, 2; Sustain 2, 3, 3.

| Area | Sort | Set | Shine | Standardise | Sustain | Weighted | Plain average |
| Machining cell 1 | 83.3% | 66.7% | 83.3% | 41.7% | 41.7% | 57.1% | 63.3% |
| Assembly bay 2 | 91.7% | 91.7% | 83.3% | 66.7% | 66.7% | 76.2% | 80.0% |

Example: Sort for machining cell 1 = (3 + 4 + 3) / (4 x 3) = 10 / 12 = 83.3 percent. Weighted total = (83.3 + 66.7 + 83.3 + 2 x 41.7 + 2 x 41.7) / 7 = 57.1 percent. The weighting by 2 for Standardise and Sustain pulls the score down because those two are weak, which is the point: they decide whether the result lasts.

## How to adapt
- Conditional formatting (Home > Conditional Formatting > Color Scales or Highlight Cells) with thresholds that your plant sets. The thresholds are your decision.
- Trend: add the audit date as a row label and use several dates in column A of Answers; change B1 to compare.
- Add a Comments column with the evidence, for example a photo reference.
- Use a Microsoft Form or Lists form to collect answers and let Power Automate append them to the Answers table.

## Common mistakes
- Dates stored as text, so the date criterion matches nothing. Check with ISNUMBER.
- S names spelled differently in Answers and in the header cells (for example Set-in-order).
- Changing the weights after the first audits without noting it. History becomes incomparable.
- Treating the percentage as a goal in itself. The audit is there to find actions.
- Using the 5S score as a substitute for tool control, FOD checks, calibration status or safety inspections. In aviation maintenance those follow their own procedures and records.

## Data protection and safety
Answers can contain names in the comment field; use roles. Scores for an area are not scores for a person. Keep the workbook where only the audit team and area leads can edit, and check with the works council how audit results are used.

title: FMEA Sheet in Excel with RPN, Tie-Break Ranking, Review Flags and Before/After Comparison
summary: Excel FMEA worksheet that calculates RPN from severity, occurrence and detection, ranks failure modes without ties, flags rows for review by severity or RPN, and compares RPN before and after actions.
body:
## What it does
A working FMEA sheet for process or design failure modes. It calculates RPN = severity x occurrence x detection, ranks the failure modes with a tie-break so that every row has a unique rank, flags rows for review using two thresholds you set, and compares the RPN before and after actions. It uses RANK, COUNTIF, SUMIFS and INDEX/MATCH, so it works in all Excel versions since 2007. One optional formula needs Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365.

## Important note on the method
RPN is the classic method. The AIAG and VDA FMEA handbook published in 2019 replaced the RPN with an Action Priority table for automotive customers. Check which method your customer, your quality system or your standard requires before you use RPN as a decision rule. RPN has known weaknesses: it is a product of ordinal ratings, different combinations give the same number, and a high-severity item with low RPN can be overlooked. That is why this sheet adds a severity flag next to the RPN.

## Layout (sheet FMEA, headers in row 1, rows 2 to 9 as example)
A ID, B Process step, C Failure mode, D Effect, E Cause, F S, G O, H D (ratings 1 to 10, with the scale of your company), I RPN, J Rank, K Flag, L Action, M S new, N O new, O D new, P RPN new.
```
I2: =F2*G2*H2
J2: =RANK(I2,I$2:I$9)+COUNTIF(I$2:I2,I2)-1
K2: =IF(OR(F2>=Settings!$B$1,I2>=Settings!$B$2),"Review","")
P2: =IF(COUNT(M2:O2)=3,M2*N2*O2,"")
```
Sheet Settings: B1 = severity review level, B2 = RPN review level. Both are your team's rules; the values below are only for the example. Results block (columns R and S):
```
S1: =SUMIFS(I2:I9,P2:P9,">0")     RPN of rows that have an action with new ratings
S2: =SUM(P2:P9)                   RPN after actions
S3: =1-S2/S1                      reduction
S4: =INDEX(C2:C9,MATCH(1,J2:J9,0))   failure mode with rank 1
S5: =COUNTIF(K2:K9,"Review")      rows to review
```
Optional sorted list (Excel 2021 or Microsoft 365): `=SORTBY(C2:C9,I2:I9,-1)` spills the failure modes in descending RPN order; ties keep their original order.

## Worked example (invented data, maintenance process)
Settings: severity level 9, RPN level 100. Ratings are examples and not a statement about any real operation.
| Step | Failure mode | S | O | D | RPN | Rank | Flag |
| Fastener torque | Wrong torque value used | 9 | 3 | 4 | 108 | 4 | Review |
| Tool control | Tool left in work area | 9 | 2 | 6 | 108 | 5 | Review |
| Calibration | Expired torque wrench used | 8 | 3 | 3 | 72 | 6 | |
| Stores | Wrong part number picked | 7 | 4 | 5 | 140 | 3 | Review |
| Work card | Step skipped | 8 | 3 | 6 | 144 | 2 | Review |
| Labelling | Label unreadable | 4 | 5 | 3 | 60 | 8 | |
| Handover | Incomplete shift handover | 6 | 5 | 6 | 180 | 1 | Review |
| Cleaning | Wrong solvent | 5 | 2 | 7 | 70 | 7 | |

Rows 1 and 2 have the same RPN of 108: RANK gives both 4, and the COUNTIF part adds 0 to the first and 1 to the second, so the ranks are 4 and 5. Five rows are flagged (two by severity 9, five by RPN of 100 or more, with overlap).

Actions with new ratings: torque card change 9, 2, 3 = 54; tool shadow board and count 9, 2, 2 = 36; barcode scan 7, 2, 2 = 28; sign-off per step 8, 2, 3 = 48; written handover template 6, 3, 3 = 54. RPN before for these five rows: 108 + 108 + 140 + 144 + 180 = 680. After: 54 + 36 + 28 + 48 + 54 = 220. Reduction = 1 - 220 / 680 = 67.6 percent. Note that severity stays 9 for the first two rows: actions that reduce occurrence or improve detection do not lower severity unless the design changes.

## How to adapt
- Insert rows inside the range (not below it) so the formulas extend.
- Put rating scales (what is a 3 for occurrence in your process) on a second sheet and link them with a note or a comment.
- Add columns for owner (role), due date and status.
- If your customer requires Action Priority, replace column I and K with a lookup table that returns the priority from S, O and D as defined in the handbook you are working with.

## Common mistakes
- Treating RPN as a measure of risk to compare across different FMEAs.
- Lowering a detection rating because a check exists on paper, without evidence that it works.
- Re-rating only the rows with actions and leaving old ratings in the comparison. The before and after sums use the same rows on purpose.
- Letting one person fill the sheet. An FMEA is a team product.
- In aviation, a sheet like this is an analysis aid. It does not replace maintenance data, work cards, the safety management system or required occurrence reporting, and certifying staff retain release responsibility.

## Data protection and safety
FMEA rows sometimes describe incidents with people involved. Describe the process, not the person. Store the file in a library with limited edit rights and version history, because the history is evidence of how the team reached its ratings.
